title: Faith and Our Practice
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: The talk highlights the importance of exploring faith in a more fundamental way, rather than seeking a single key or understanding that explains life's mysteries. Instead, faith can be cultivated through practice, such as zazen, where one embodies Buddha's law and enacts the Dharma for the benefit of all beings. By letting go of fixed views and self-concept, and trusting ourselves, each other, and the practice itself, we can allow Buddha's expression to flow through us and awaken to a deeper understanding of reality.

sentences.text: I've been thinking a little more lately about faith, faith in our practice.
When I first got interested in Buddhism, or stumbled into Buddhism, I didn't have any religious background, and the word faith seemed like the one that the Christians had an exclusive license to.
So I never really thought about this word faith.
But then later I learned there's a traditional Japanese Zen teaching that there are three essential practices in Zen.
Faith, they say great faith; great doubt, which is a puzzler, interesting, challenging; and great determination, or sometimes they say great confidence.
So I've been speaking about this a little bit and continuing to explore it, and I want to explore a little more tonight.
One thing that I have shared a couple of times that [unclear: "Bear is repeating"] is from the wonderful recent book that Sallie Tisdale made of her teacher Kyogen Carlson's teachings.
I forget the title right now.
He was one of our dear Dharma neighbors to the south, in Portland, who has since passed on, actually a couple of years ago.
Anyway, there was a talk in there by Kyogen about faith, and it has this one paragraph that really stirs the pot for me.
See if it does for you too.
Kyogen said:

*In the world of spirituality, there's something I call the illusion of a key, the illusion that there's a code to life, a code to the world, and if we just had that key, it would all make sense, key like in a lock.
This illusion tells us that our suffering would go away when we would figure it all out.
A lot of storylines we add to religion have to do with this hope for a key.
I do believe that things beyond our comprehension do happen and they can be significant and meaningful, but they don't explain everything.
They don't give us that key.*

So obviously the suggestion is that maybe there's some idea that we just have a very special experience, or a deep realization, or learn the right thing, read the most inspiring and amazing book, or hear the best talk, or find the best teacher, and we'll get this key.
And that we will search in vain.
There is no such key.
I always figure with a teaching like this that it doesn't mean it might not be an important and central part of your practice to look for the key.
Maybe it really motivates us, maybe for a long time, to seek and practice and learn if we think there's a key, even if we know there kind of isn't.
That's just how we are.
We have to stick to something a long time sometimes before we let it go.
Just because some guy reads a paragraph from a book doesn't mean we're going to change.
That would be just like another key.
There's no key to help you learn there's no key.
But what's funny about him saying this is it doesn't tell us what to have faith in.
It maybe suggests what not to have faith in, or not to be fixated on.

And maybe it also says to really practice with noticing and paying attention, to when, either consciously or subconsciously or half-consciously, your desire and your search and your belief in a key drives you.
It drives your behavior, your thinking, your understanding, your assumptions.
Because it's a deeply held view, I think, for many of us, all of us.
It's kind of "if only."
If only we could figure it out, figure ourselves out, figure out how to talk to people so that they'll agree with us.
Figure out a world that's sensible and reasonable and kind, well-planned, not self-destructive.
There's got to be a way to do this, but it seems like there isn't.
This desire for everything to make sense and to be reasonable doesn't ever quite work that way, does it?
And yet it's also not the opposite of that, right?
The world is not in utter chaos.
There are patterns and order and predictable things, apparently.
There are describable things and scientific laws and so on that are mostly true.
So the world makes sense and it also doesn't make sense.
That's really hard for us to hold.
We make sense and we don't make sense.
We try to understand.
We can understand and we can't understand.
Which, of course, our now beloved Diamond Sutra told us about a thousand million times, right?
Could be there's a bit of social pressure to claim that you like the Diamond Sutra, but that's another subject.
Maybe you hated it.
But anyway, what to have faith in?
If we can't have faith in a key, or some kind of order or some kind of consistent something, can we have faith in goodness?
I'm not really sure.
And is it a faith that requires an object, this great faith?
Does it need to be faith in something?
Or is it free of needing to be connected in that way?
Is it an objectless faith, an open faith, an empty faith?
But if we want to explore having faith in something, we could explore having faith in the three jewels, which aren't exactly objects anyway.
So faith in the Buddha.
Makes sense.
Faith in the awakened one.
Faith in awakening itself.
Confidence, right?
Confidence that we really can be more open, more clear, more understanding, more accepting, less caught, less tight, less triggered.
And this is not, I think, too hard, because we all experience moving up and down and back and forth on some kind of continuum in this area.
Sometimes we're lost in confusion.
We all experience this.
Other times we're more clear, grounded, open.
So if awakening has something to do with that, we all experience it in a matter of degree.
So faith in Buddha seems like it has some experience behind it, even if we would never be so audacious as to say, "I am enlightened," or something.
But we all experience enlightenment.
There's evidence in our experience.
Because it just stands to reason that if we are sometimes, some days, some moments, more settled, more open and more aware, that could be more.
We could go further.
We could be even more aware, even more open, even more insightful, even more truly here.
And just keep going, right?
Just keep going endlessly.
We say practice is endless.
Of course, this makes you remember that there are endless debates in the tradition about sudden and gradual shifts in awakening, if that's the right word to use.
But probably it's really a both-and kind of thing.
There is a gradual dawning of light, with plenty of setbacks along the way.
We've all seen this.
And there are sudden moments when it's like the veil drops, and everything feels different.
This also happens.

But probably it's making the Buddha too small, and not being true to the Buddha or having full faith in the Buddha, to only cast the process of awakening as a psychological, observable process that we can describe and talk about.
There must be so much more, right?
Because anything we can talk about, or make sense of, put into a conceptual framework, that can't quite be Buddha, could it?
It's all in the realm of conditioned thinking.
So faith in Buddha must also, or interpenetratedly, be faith in a life unbounded by any such ideas as confusion or clarity or insight.
It's got to be bigger than even that, right?
Can you feel a little glimmer of that possibility when you think about this?
This feeling and living into and being in the reality way beyond whatever it is that we call reality, way bigger, more than whatever we could call it.
And of course then we think about the Diamond Sutra again, which always reminds us: yeah, but you've got to call it something.
So this is worth thinking about, for each of us, I think, or feeling into.
What is your feeling about awakening?
About Buddha?
What draws you to practice in this way of Buddha?
Why are you here anyway?
I don't know if I have a good answer.
I don't know if it's an answerable question.
That's a good question.
Why are you practicing?
What is Buddha to you?
Does faith mean we can't really talk about it?
I have more questions and answers for sure.
And then the Dharma, the second jewel, with much overlap here with Buddha: the path, the teachings, the way, what we practice.
Faith in Dharma is confidence, even when we don't really understand it.
We don't really understand what we're doing or what we're studying in that usual way of understanding, of sense-making, exactly because there's no key, right?
But we have some sense of it.
We do this, we do that, we come to the zendo, sit on our cushions, we study, we chant.
So there seems to be some kind of Dharma here, some kind of path.
And as with Buddha, we have some experience to back us up, maybe.
But I don't know if our describable experience is really quite Dharma in its entirety.
Probably not.
Our Soto school especially emphasizes that Buddha and Dharma are really just two ways of talking about the same thing somehow.
So this phrase comes up all the time: Buddha Dharma, Buddha dash Dharma, or one word, Buddhadharma.
And Dogen's phrase, practice enlightenment, practice enlightenment, Dharma Buddha.
So do we have faith in Dharma?
Sitting in zazen does seem to be an expression of practice enlightenment, of Dharma Buddha.
And even so, at first, it seems like something we sit down and do.
It doesn't seem like it actually is something that we do, and definitely not something that we do to get somewhere or get something or figure something out, like becoming Buddha.
The actual feeling is more like zazen is Buddha Dharma.
Dharma Buddha is zazen.
Chris and I and probably others have over the years quoted from a really great teacher in our lineage, a current teacher, Taigen Dan Leighton.
He teaches in Chicago, a student of Reb Anderson, San Francisco Zen Center.
Really lovely guy too, if you ever get to meet him.
Anyway, I bring him up because Taigen wrote a really important essay that now everyone associates with him, called "Zazen as Enactment Ritual."

Saying, with great scholarly clarity and lots of quotations from teachers, Dogen primarily and many teachers that preceded and followed Dogen, and saying really from his heart, deeply from his heart, that zazen is exactly not a means to an end, not something that fixes us up.
And not even in the sort of clever way of, "Well, if I let go of getting something in zazen, then cool, I'll get something," which is just getting something, right?
Taigen's teaching and reading of Dogen and these other key teachers is that there is absolutely no getting to be got.
And that this is especially wonderful and freeing because it helps us realize there's no getter.
There's no getter to get the stuff.
There's only practice, and that practice needs to be expressed with a body.
So it has a form.
And in the world of form, which is the world of ritual, that's where we could get mixed up, because we do it with the body.
So we see each other doing it.
We can explain how to do it: you do this, you do that.
We can't help but use pronouns like you and me and them.
So an embodied ritual, an embodied enactment, could easily confuse us into thinking that somebody's doing something to get something.
Because, yeah, it's kind of dumb to do something you don't get anything from, right?
Makes me think there was a period when Norman used to say, "You want to know what's great about zazen?"
And we'd all say, "What?
What?
What?"
He said, "It's absolutely useless.
That's what's good about it."

Which is fun and provocative, but I think also really a smart way of talking, because it helps us see how in our conditioned lives we're so addicted to utility that the word useless, not having utility, has become a bad thing.
It's not inherently that way.
We just linked it up.
So anyway, we think of zazen as meditation and that it has some kind of benefits.
And it does.
But looking at it at first, we might think, well, you do the zazen to get the stuff.
And that's the beautiful thing that makes sense in all cultures and is scientifically valid.
And then after that, we do some ritual because that's a custom and a tradition and we want to be respectful, and they'd probably be annoyed with me if I said let's not do that anymore.
Or it's nice, I like it, or I don't like it.
But actually the teaching and the understanding in the tradition, as Taigen is reminding us, is that it's all ritual.
One hundred percent of everything is ritual, including our so-called regular lives.
Zazen is the ritual of Buddha practicing the Dharma.
And when we sit, we're enacting, that's the verb Taigen used, which I think is really thoughtful.
The essay is called "Zazen as Enactment Ritual."
So when we sit, we're enacting Buddha.
Enacting has the same root as acting, like playing a part, but it actually has a different meaning.
It's from the legal tradition, legal and government.
Legislation is enacted to define the law, right?
And it's an old tradition in Zen to use legal language.
The word koan means a public case, like a legal precedent.
A precedent of awakening is a koan.
And the Dharma is called the law, capital L, usually.
So in zazen, we are laying down the law, enacting Buddha's law, Buddha's Dharma, for the good of all beings, which is why you have laws, right?
The laws are for the good of the many.
So this law is for the good of all beings.
And there's a great eighteenth-century Japanese monk, a Soto reformer, called Menzon Zuiho.
He's an important figure, especially to the Dogen studies people, because Menzon really revived the study of Dogen in Japan in the first half of the eighteenth century.
Because it turns out, this is an interesting historical note, that in the centuries after Dogen, six or so centuries, nobody much read him.
Nobody read Dogen's words.
He was revered as an ancestor, and his writings were revered as sacred objects, the scrolls, the different fascicles of the Shobogenzo and all the different writings of Dogen.
Different temples in Japan have this copy or that copy, and there weren't that many copies.
They were taken out on special days, or maybe actually in Japanese religion, a lot of the time, the really sacred stuff is never seen.
It's always hidden away.
So maybe it was kept hidden in the treasury or behind the altar.
They have the public altar you can see, and then there are secret altars in the back.
It's actually an American conceit that Zen is simple.
Go to Japan, you find out it's not simple.

So anyway, I remember learning this, and I remember at the time, without really thinking about it, applying our typical Western "what do you get out of it" view to that and thinking to myself, well, isn't that silly?
Isn't that kind of superstitious?
Just like religion, to not actually study the great teacher's words.
But I don't know if I quite feel that way now.
Also a beautiful practice of faith.
And I'm all for the both-and anyway: to have faith in the sacred objects and the fascinating teachings within them.
But anyway, this is really great.
Taigen quotes Menzon in his essay.
So this is Taigen with quotations from Menzon:
*Menzon critiques the dualistic meditation of those who aspire to rid themselves of delusion and gain enlightenment.
For this is nothing but creating the karma of acceptance and rejection.*
It's really important, I think.
Menzon is saying that those who aspire to rid themselves of delusion and gain enlightenment, that's terrible, because it's creating the karma of acceptance and rejection.
It's reinforcing these dualistic notions that we all get lost in.
Taigen goes on:
*For Menzon, on the other hand, quote, "Zazen is not a practice for getting rid of delusions and gaining enlightenment."
Commenting on a teaching attributed to the third ancestor, Menzon adds, "If you do not make mental struggle, the darkness itself becomes self-illumination of the light.
If you do not make mental struggle, the*
darkness itself becomes the self-illumination of light.
And later he says, this is the culmination of the Buddha way and the unsurpassable samadhi, which is continuously going beyond.
I hear that phrase a lot: continuously going beyond.
For this reason, all Buddhas in the world of the ten directions always dwell in Zazen.
That's also a great verb, to dwell in Zazen, to live here.

This is a fascinating thought, that we could just end up reinforcing the karma of acceptance and rejection, the way we put ourselves on this endless hamster wheel, right, of wanting this and not wanting that in all its many, many, many, many forms.
Not a path to freedom, that.
So we have faith in Zazen, it seems.
Zazen is dwelling place.
Zazen is enactment.
Zazen is expression of awakening and the path to awakening, all just right there, merged, not separate.
Dogen says the minute you sit down, right, the minute that you sit down, you're already enlightened, and before that and after that, too.
So what was your experience this evening in Zazen?
Were you allowing this enactment to flow through you, allowing Buddha to express?
I felt really agitated tonight, in the subjective way that we look at our experience.
I felt agitated and a little discombobulated, a little rushed.
There's a little impact in my psyche of realizing I had the Zoom set up all wrong and you guys weren't here.
Well, you were, I wasn't, somebody wasn't here.
I don't know, who knows where is where.
It took a while to settle down.
So we do Zazen with our conditioned body and mind, but I was thinking about this and trying to feel into this even as I felt sort of agitated and unsettled, which I don't prefer.
The karma I have accrued of acceptance and rejection wants to reject feeling agitated, especially when doing the holy, holy rituals of Zazen, and at the Zendo and with everybody, blah, blah, blah.
I really experimented with: can I just invite a feeling, a notion?
I don't know what word to use, but this is Buddha expressing too.
Sometimes people talk like, yeah, you can be nervous Buddha, you can be angry Buddha, you can be this Buddha, that Buddha.
That's okay, I think.
It's not really a weird thing.
It's some kind of inner turning or inner shift we allow.
We invite, we get curious about.
It just happens if we get out of the way, even when we're stumbling over ourselves internally.
And so we make an effort.
We always make an effort, a gentle effort.
There's some mechanical technique stuff we all know about.
It helps to be grounded in your breathing and feeling the breath, especially low down in the belly and the [unclear: "hot eye"].
The Dan Tian, the Chinese would say.
To notice the mind wandering and gently coming back, as if we were ever going anywhere.
But it's not just that, is it?
It's more than that and exactly less than that.
I think maybe what Zazen is is a gentle effort to get out of our own way, to get out of Buddha's way.
We do need our body and our mind and our heart to facilitate, to channel maybe this enactment of Buddha.
But we don't make it happen.
We can't make it happen.
Maybe we can allow it to happen.
But the effort is so gentle that it's almost not even effort.
I like that second point by Menzon: if you don't make mental struggle, stop struggling.
If you stop fighting, darkness itself becomes the self-illumination of the light.
So self-healing.
This is like another description of that great phrase.
I think Chris and several people did some talks about this, maybe Thales too.
Jijuju zanmai, self-fulfilling samadhi.
It's not a manufactured thing.
We all experience shifts and changes in Zazen, and maybe from time to time you notice, we all notice, there's something going on here far more than just me trying to do Zazen.
It seems like I need to be here because I can't not be here.
But Zazen is doing Zazen.
At least for a moment Buddha expresses through us.
And that's beyond beautiful.
It doesn't depend on us being calm and peaceful and finding the key.
Here's another example of no key.
There's no key to Zazen, although it sure does help to do the darn thing a lot.
We've been thinking about sesshin lately, with Samish sesshin apparently happening and people are signing up.
I think there's like 30-something people signed up, maybe, huh?
Yeah.
It'll be a full sesshin.
Come if you can.
One of the great virtues of sesshin is we do so much Zazen, right?
In a particular context and container that's really supportive.
So maybe we can't make Zazen happen, but we can support Zazen happening.
Especially in sesshin, I think, you just sit long enough, day after day, that eventually, just organically, you, if it's even you, just get tired of being in your own way and you fall away.
You get tired of being your nutty self.
It's so exhausting that eventually it quiets down.
Maybe it gradually quiets down, gradual, right?
Maybe it just kind of blips off for a little bit.
What a relief to enact Buddha in that way.
But all this talk is so kind of tricky.
It can just feed back on itself.
Maybe it's actually a problem to use a word like awakening, because it sounds like there's someone, me, you, who was not awake before.
And then they did a thing and now they're awake.
So they are awakening.
So we probably need a different word.
I don't know.
Maybe no word is quite right, so it's what we got.
But maybe forgetting is better.

Practice the deep Dharma of forgetting: forgetting our ideas of our separateness, forgetting our projections, forgetting to cling, forgetting all about our fixed views about what's supposed to happen and who's supposed to do it and how they're supposed to do it, and forgetting the key, right?
Forgetting the search for the key.
But maybe Zazen helps us forget in a really good form of forgetting.
Dogen uses the term famously in Genjokoan: "To study the way is to study the self."
Remember what the study of the self is?
To forget the self.
And so we sit down, and maybe that's our core practice.
If I was actually from New York, I could say this right, but maybe our core practice is like, forget about it.
But our habit energy of self is really strong.

How can anything that you can't even see, just made of, maybe it's made of neuronal patterns or something, how can it be that the pattern of self and the impulse of self has that much momentum, that much power?
It's really incredible.
We could really harness the power of the self energy.
We could [unclear: "feel, you know, power of the world easily"].
So the self concept keeps coming back in its many manifestations as we practice, as we live: opinions, judgments, assumptions, presumptions, projections, they keep coming back.
But we're so lucky that we have a framework, a way of noticing that and practicing with it.
So maybe what we really have faith in is a process, a way of practice.
Here's another way of talking about Dharma: self keeps coming back.
We keep sitting down and forgetting about it, and it keeps coming back.
So faith in Buddha, Dharma, faith in practice, enlightenment, and for sure, we talk a lot about this, faith in the wondrous context in which all this happens.
Faith in sangha.
There's the obvious sangha of us guys, who come together on the screen and in the room to practice this.
And there's the many, many bigger layers of sangha, of community radiating out to beings and universes.
But it's a little more tangible to think about the active practice community here, what we call the sangha.
It's really separate individuals, isn't it?
But we call it the sangha.
So can we have faith in that?
Faith in that means faith in us, right?
Actually means faith in us.
This is a really active thing to practice with.
It's hard sometimes, and it's easy sometimes.
We can for sure feel and express and receive and give a lot of appreciation.
There's a lot of appreciation and warmth, I think, in this community, which is really wonderful, like amazing.
And we're also for sure a collection of easily confused, opinionated humans.
Sometimes that faith gets a little ragged, or falls away altogether.
But here's something I thought about when I was thinking about this that seems really key.
When each of us is practicing faith in sangha, can we completely include ourselves?
I'm sangha too.
So it's faith in each other, and it's faith in ourselves, these selves that we are wanting to forget.
Faith in that.
So, a wonderful place for practice enlightenment.
Our faith in ourselves is a faith in itself that's not what we think it is either.
It's growing, it's changing, it's so radically impermanent, more than we can even think about.
We nurture ourselves because we suffer, but not because there's something wrong with us. [unclear: "Course condition being suffer"], that's natural.
So here we have in here and out there.
Here's the other people, I don't know if you can see very well, and the many people on the list and in our hearts that aren't here tonight.
This practice of faith in sangha includes really studying the feeling when that faith falters, when we get frustrated with each other.
Maybe what's really important then is to study that when we get frustrated with each other, we're actually getting frustrated with ourselves.
I think that old saw about what bugs you in someone else is actually what bugs you in you.
I think it's unavoidably true.
So a deep practice for us here, joyful, challenging, deeply responsible practice, precepts practice at its core, and a faith in this as a process too that runs the whole gamut, right?
Sangha can be a joyful party.
We like that.
And it can also be the uncomfortable experience of being tossed in a rock polisher and rubbed around, feeling our sharp edges.
I don't think it probably feels very good to be a rock in a rock polisher, right?
Ouch.
But maybe we do end up shiny and beautiful.
But yeah, hard to let ourselves be rubbed smooth.
We resist it.
We've discovered that we're protecting all kinds of things.
So sangha is such a huge realm of faith.
Sometimes it's also just too much and no longer feels right for somebody to be formally in the sangha.
This is an interesting thing to have faith in too: when people who seem like core members of the family leave, or since we weren't actually living together, it's really not like they leave, actually.
It's more like one day, usually without preamble or warning, they just don't come anymore.
They stop coming.
I've noticed another example of that recently, and I've seen it before.
I'm sure you have too.
It's confusing.
It's a challenge to the faith practice in sangha.
Our conditioned minds suffer.
Is there something wrong?
There's something wrong with the way we do things.
There's something wrong with me.
Is there something wrong with the person who left?
Is this something I said or did or didn't do or didn't notice?
Is there something in my blind spot?
And there may well have been, for sure.
Most often we probably will never know.

Oddly, my experience, I think more and more, I'm starting to understand this a little more, is that that too polishes us, softens us, helps us to practice acceptance, to practice humility, to practice letting go.
Although sometimes it takes a long time to accept, I think, when somebody stops coming that we really thought was really in it with us and in a strong relationship with us.
But actually even their leaving is a gift, and their coming is a gift if they ever come back.
And really, the more I think about it, I don't like the rock tumbler analogy anyway.
We're not rocks.
We're soft.
We're vulnerable.
So I don't know what the metaphor is for being together in a way that leaves us softer and even more vulnerable.
But probably not a rock polisher or a potato washing tub.
Because for sure, the long-term result of this thing, this practice, this faith, is love, is love.
And how can we not have faith in something that brings love?
So, this being the day of Saint Patrick, I thought we'd close with a little bit of faith from Saint Patrick.
I did a little reminding myself about Saint Patrick, beyond just green and no pinching.
I don't know if he really liked the color green.
I think that'll never be known.
I won't say too much about him because we're out of time, but he was born in the fifth century of the common era in Roman Britain.
He was actually enslaved when he was 16 years old and spent six years from there living as a slave, suffering as a slave.
Then he had a vision that helped him escape from slavery.
The slavers took him to Ireland, took him to Ireland, and he eventually got back home to his family.
But something had turned in him.
Some faith had arisen in him in his years of captivity and inspired him.
He was from a church family.

His father and uncle and something were priests, so it's not too surprising, but his years as a slave inspired him to be a priest, to be a teacher, and, as you know, to go to Ireland, right back to the place of his misery, to practice and share his Dharma.
Two texts are attributed to him.
They're not really sure if he wrote them both.
And a couple of prayers.
So here's one of the couple of prayers that's preserved from Saint Patrick.
This is our Saint Patrick's Day celebration.
*I arise today through a mighty strength, the invocation of the Trinity, through belief in the threeness, through confession in the oneness of the creator of creation.

I arise today through the strength of Christ's birth and his baptism, to the strength of his crucifixion and his burial, to the strength of his resurrection and his ascension, to the strength of his descent and his judgment of doom.

I arise today through the strength of love of cherubim, in obedience of angels, in service of archangels, in hope of resurrection to meet with reward, in the prayers of patriarchs and the predictions of prophets, in the preachings of apostles, in the faith of confessors, in the deeds of righteous, of the righteous ones.*

*I arise today through the strength of heaven, the light of the sun, the radiance of the moon, the splendor of fire, the speed of lightning, the swiftness of wind, the depth of the sea, the stability of the earth, the firmness of rock.

I arise today through God's strength to pilot me, God's might to uphold me, God's wisdom to guide me, God's eye to look before me, God's ear to hear me, God's word to speak for me, God's hand to guard me, God's shield to protect me, God's host to save me.

From snares of devils, from temptation of vices, from everyone who shall wish me ill, afar and near, I summon today all these powers between me and those evils, against every cruel and merciless power that may oppose body and soul, against incantations and false prophets and black laws and false laws and crafts and spells, against every knowledge that corrupts body and soul.
Christ shield me today against poison, against burning, against drowning, against wounding, so that there may come to me an abundance.*

*Christ with me, Christ before me, Christ behind me, Christ in me, Christ beneath me, Christ above me, Christ on my right, Christ on my left, Christ when I lie down, Christ when I sit down, Christ when I arise, Christ in the heart of every man who thinks of me, Christ in the mouth of everyone who speaks of me, Christ in every eye that sees me, Christ in every ear that hears me.
I arise today through a mighty strength, the invocation of the Trinity, through belief in the threeness, through confession of the oneness and the creator of creation.*
Far out stuff.
And lots of faith.
All right, thanks for all that.
Our intention equally extend to every being and place [unclear: "with the true"].
I guess put this back in the pillar there.

verbatim.text: I've been thinking a little more lately about faith, faith in our practice, which you know, when I first got interested in Buddhism or stumbled into Buddhism, I didn't have any religious background and the word faith seemed like the one that the Christians like had an exclusive license to.
